For as long as software has been sold on physical or digital media, a global underground network of reverse-engineers, coders, and digital archivists has worked to unlock it. What began in the late 1970s as high schoolers trading copied cassette tapes in local computer clubs evolved into a highly secretive, competitive, global counterculture known simply as The Scene.
This is the complete history of video game piracy—tracing its technological evolution, the mechanics of how game cracks actually work, the escalation of anti-piracy protections, and the intense human drama that defines its modern era.
1. The Dawn Era (1970s–1980s):
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Physical Media and Copy Protection
In the late 1970s and early 1980s, games were distributed on physical formats like audio cassette tapes (for systems like the Commodore PET and ZX Spectrum) and 5.25-inch floppy disks (for the Apple II and Commodore 64).
Early game developers quickly realized that standard disk drives could read and write arbitrary data, making raw magnetic disk-to-disk copying effortless.
The First Anti-Piracy Protections
To stop users from making duplicate floppy disks using basic software, game publishers began engineering physical and magnetic hurdles:
Custom Sector Formatting: Publishers modified disk drives to write data to non-standard sectors, out-of-bounds tracks, or deliberately corrupted sector headers. Standard copy utilities could not duplicate these irregular physical markers.
*Manual & Code-Wheel Checks*: Games presented interactive physical checks upon startup. A game might ask: "Enter the 4th word on page 12, line 3 of the instruction manual." Others included layered, rotating cardboard "code wheels" or sheets printed on dark blue paper that could not be photocopied.
The Birth of "The Scene"
To defeat these manual checks and custom sector locks, computer hobbyists began forming organized underground groups. Teams like *Dynamic Duo*, *FairLight*, and *International Network of Crackers (INC)* emerged.
These groups competed fiercely to be the "FIRST" to release a working copy of a commercial game. This competitive underground ecosystem became known as *The Scene*.
2. The Golden Age of Warez and the Art of the "Cracktro"
By the 1990s, with the rise of MS-DOS, Amiga, and early Windows PCs, game piracy shifted from physical tape/disk swapping to digital Bulletin Board Systems (BBS) and early Internet protocols (FTP, IRC, and Usenet).
Scene Culture and Hierarchy
The Scene operated under strict, unwritten rules. It was never intended for the general public; it was an exclusive, highly secretive club built around speed, skill, and bragging rights.
```
[ The Scene Supply Chain ]
[ Suppliers ] ──► Acquire unreleased retail/press copies of games
│
▼
[ Crackers ] ──► Reverse-engineer protection, strip DRM, modify code
│
▼
[ Couriers ] ──► Upload cracked releases to high-speed private "Topsites"
│
▼
[ P2P / Web ] ──► Leaked down to public Torrent sites, Usenet, and forums

```
Suppliers: Individuals working at retail stores, game development studios, pressing plants, or software review magazines who secured pre-release or day-one physical copies.
*Crackers*: The elite reverse-engineers who defeated the game’s protection mechanisms.
*Topsites*:Ultra-fast, highly encrypted private FTP servers hosted on university or corporate backbones where releases were traded using credit systems.
*Couriers*: Fast-upload bots and humans who raced to spread releases across Topsites to earn uploading rank.
Cracktros, NFOs, and Keygens
When a scene group cracked a game, they didn’t just strip the protection—they branded the executable file.
 *The Cracktro (Crack Intro):
Before the main game booted, crackers injected an intro screen. These cracktros featured custom assembly-coded 3D visual effects, rotating logos, and infectious 8-bit chiptune music created by demoscene musicians.
*NFO Files:
Plain-text informational files included with every release. Formatted with intricate ASCII art, NFOs contained system requirements, installation instructions, group member shout-outs, and aggressive "GREETZ" or "DISSETZ" targeted at rival cracking crews.
*Keygens (Key Generators):
Instead of modifying the game’s code directly, some crackers reverse-engineered the mathematical algorithm used to validate license keys. They then wrote a standalone application—accompanied by signature chip-music—that generated valid serial numbers indefinitely.
3. How Game Cracking Works Under the Hood
To understand how a game crack works, one must look at how software executes at the hardware level. Games are compiled from high-level programming languages (C++, C#) into raw machine code executed by the CPU.
When a game includes Digital Rights Management (DRM), it periodically checks whether a valid license, optical disc, or account token exists. If the check returns **FALSE**, the code routes the CPU to terminate the program.
Step 1: Reverse Engineering & Disassembly
Crackers use disassemblers and debuggers such as *IDA Pro*, *Ghidra*, *x64dbg*, or *x32dbg* to convert binary executable files (.exe or .dll) back into human-readable Assembly language (x86 or x64).
```assembly
; Example of a basic, uncracked license check in x86 Assembly:
CALL CheckLicenseToken ; Query platform or disk for license
CMP EAX, 0 ; Check if return code is 0 (0 = Invalid / Unlicensed)
JE BlockAccess ; Jump to termination routine IF Equal to 0
CALL StartGame ; Otherwise, proceed to load game engine
```
Step 2: Code Patching (NOPing and Conditional Branching)
To bypass simple license checks, a cracker identifies the conditional jump instruction in assembly (JE - Jump if Equal, JNE - Jump if Not Equal) and modifies the raw hex bytes of the binary:
*Overwriting with NOPs*: The cracker replaces the conditional check bytes with 0x90 (NOP or "No Operation"). The CPU skips the license evaluation entirely and executes straight into the game.
*Inverting Jumps*: Changing a JE (Jump if Equal) to a JMP (Unconditional Jump) forces the execution path into the StartGame routine, regardless of whether a valid key exists.
```assembly
; Example of a patched (cracked) routine:
CALL CheckLicenseToken
CMP EAX, 0
NOP ; Overwritten: CPU ignores check result
NOP ; Overwritten: Execution flows straight through
CALL StartGame ; Game loads successfully
```
Step 3: Steam API Emulation
Modern digital storefronts like Steam, Epic Games, and EA Desktop do not rely solely on simple executable checks. Instead, games call external software development kit (SDK) functions (e.g., steam_api64.dll) to verify ownership.
Instead of modifying hundreds of individual code checks inside the main game executable, crackers write a custom *Steam API Emulator*. This is a modified .dll file dropped into the game folder that intercepts calls intended for the official Steam client:
```
[ Legitimate Game Flow ]
Game.exe ──► Calls steam_api64.dll ──► Queries Steam Client ──► License Validated
[ Cracked Game Flow ]
Game.exe ──► Calls Emulator steam_api64.dll ──► Fake Response (Owner = True) ──► Game Starts
```
The emulator responds to every query with fake positive responses, telling the game engine that the user owns all DLCs, is connected to legitimate servers, and holds a valid license.
4. The DRM Arms Race: From SecuROM to Always-Online
As games moved to CD-ROMs and PC gaming exploded in the late 1990s and 2000s, publishers realized simple executable checks were insufficient. This launched a decades-long technological escalation.
| Era / Technology | Operational Mechanism | How Crackers Defeated It |
|---|---|---|
| **SafeDisc** | Wrote intentional read errors onto specific tracks of physical CDs. | Modded optical drives and emulation software (Daemon Tools, Alcohol 120%) that forged sub-channel data. |
| **SecuROM** | Analyzed physical disc properties, such as data density and laser read timing gaps (Data Position Measurement). | Low-level ring-0 kernel drivers, memory patching, and loader scripts that hid virtual drive software. |
| **StarForce** | Installed deep kernel-level device drivers that took control of the IDE/SATA bus to inspect optical hardware. | Physically unplugging optical drive cables, system driver cleansers, and custom ring-0 kernel hooks. |
| **Always-Online DRM** | Required a continuous internet connection to offload vital game logic to remote publisher servers (e.g., *SimCity 2013*, *Diablo III*). | Writing custom local server emulators that mimicked publisher backends, or reverse-engineering server-side calculations. |
5. The Denuvo Era: The Wall That Changed Everything
In 2014, an Austrian company called *Denuvo Software Solutions* launched *Denuvo Anti-Tamper**. It fundamentally changed the game piracy ecosystem.
Denuvo is not a standalone DRM system. Instead, it acts as an ultra-complex protective shell wrapped around existing DRMs like Steam, Epic, or EA.
Why Denuvo Is So Difficult to Defeat
1. *Code Virtualization*:
Denuvo converts native x86/x64 machine code into a proprietary, non-standard instruction set. It then executes this code inside an internal virtual machine runtime. To reverse-engineer it, crackers must first manually map and reconstruct the entire custom virtual architecture from scratch.
2. *Massive Obfuscation*:
Denuvo bloats executable files, inserting millions of junk instructions, false code paths, and self-decrypting routines to exhaust disassemblers like IDA Pro.
3. *Dynamic Hardware Tokens*: Denuvo generates an encrypted hardware fingerprint based on the user’s specific CPU, GPU, and motherboard. It contacts Denuvo authentication servers online to fetch a unique, time-sensitive activation token.
4. *Continuous Triggers*: Denuvo places thousands of hidden "triggers" throughout the game loop. If a player reaches Chapter 3, fires a weapon, or opens an inventory menu, Denuvo silently re-verifies the hardware token. If a crack is imperfect, the game crashes hours into gameplay.
When Denuvo debuted, classic scene groups (such as *RELOADED*, *SKIDROW*, and *FAIRLIGHT*) found their traditional reverse-engineering tools rendered completely useless. Games that used to be cracked within hours went uncracked for months—or years.
6. Key Figures, Drama, and the Modern Scene
As traditional scene groups retired or surrendered in the face of Denuvo, the vacuum was filled by isolated, highly unconventional individuals.
The Rise and Fall of Voksi (2016–2018)
Press enter or click to view image in full size

A young Bulgarian programmer operating under the alias *Voksi* (founder of the group REVOLT) made waves by creating clever runtime memory bypasses for Denuvo titles. Rather than fully cracking the DRM, Voksi’s tools tricked Denuvo’s servers using legitimate steam demo licenses to fetch real hardware activation tokens.
In summer 2018, Denuvo filed a formal criminal complaint with the Bulgarian Ministry of Interior. Bulgarian cybercrime police raided Voksi’s home, seizing his servers and computers, ending his cracking career at age 21.
The CPY and CODEX Dominance
For several years, the Italian scene group *CPY* (Steampunks) and the veteran group *CODEX* intermittently unlocked Denuvo titles through painstaking, brute-force virtualization analysis. However, by 2022, CODEX officially announced their retirement, citing that modern games no longer offered the fun, competitive scene environment of the past.
The EMPRESS Era ($500 Commissions and Wild Manifestos)
By 2020, virtually only one person in the world was actively and consistently cracking modern versions of Denuvo: a mysterious, volatile individual operating under the moniker *EMPRESS*.
EMPRESS broke almost every traditional rule of The Scene:
Monetization:
While traditional Scene rules strictly prohibited taking money, EMPRESS established a crowdfunding model—requiring a *$500 cryptocurrency bounty* to crack a specific requested game.
